extracted.intended_audience: IP professionals, policymakers, researchers, national/regional IP offices and applicants
extracted.subtask_short: overview of patent and IP systems
extracted.subtask_description: A concise authoritative overview and glossary describing the major IP systems (patents, utility models, trademarks, industrial designs, GIs, plant variety rights) and the legal/technical criteria, procedural phases, and statistical counting conventions relevant to filing, grant and protection. Useful for practitioners, policymakers and analysts needing standards and definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentable invention must meet the standards of novelty, non-obviousness (inventive step) and industrial applicability; elsewhere phrased as the invention must be novel, involve an inventive step and be industrially applicable, as judged by a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents grant exclusive rights for a limited period (generally 20 years) in return for disclosure of the invention. National/regional patent offices decide patentability according to national law. The PCT system facilitates multi-jurisdictional filing but substantive grant remains with national/regional offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent disclosure obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants are obliged to disclose their inventions to the public so that they may be replicated by others skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure is a condition for receiving patent rights; for biological inventions involving microorganisms, disclosure can require a deposit under the Budapest Treaty (see IDA entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term and territoriality
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are valid for a limited period (generally 20 years) and patent rights are limited to the jurisdiction of the issuing authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To obtain protection in multiple jurisdictions applicants must file in each jurisdiction (national route) or use international systems (PCT) that simplify timing but do not override national grant decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT procedure phases
rubrics_metrics.description: The PCT application process begins with an international phase (international search and optional preliminary and supplementary international examination) and concludes with the national phase, during which national/regional patent offices decide on patentability according to national law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PCT delays the requirement to file separate national applications but does not grant patents itself; further information at www.wipo.int/pct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility models confer rights similar to patents but differ in terms and conditions: typically issued for a shorter period (6–10 years) and in most offices protection is granted without substantive examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedures for granting UMs are governed by national IP offices and rights are territorially limited. The report uses 'utility model' to include similar short-term protections such as short-term patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budapest Treaty microorganism deposit requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: When an invention involves microorganisms and disclosure in writing is insufficient, national laws in most countries require the applicant to deposit a sample at a designated International Depositary Authority (IDA). Under the Budapest Treaty a deposit with any IDA suffices for national procedures in contracting states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An IDA is a scientific institution (typically a culture collection) capable of storing microorganisms; deposit eliminates the need to deposit in every country where protection is sought. See www.wipo.int/treaties/en/registration/budapest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark function and territoriality
rubrics_metrics.description: A trademark is a sign used to distinguish the goods or services of one enterprise from those of another and gives the holder the exclusive right to use the mark for the goods/services for which it is registered; rights are limited to the jurisdiction of the registering authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trademark registrations can be maintained indefinitely by paying renewal fees; registration procedures are governed by national/regional IP offices. Service marks and trademarks are treated under the generic term 'trademark' in the report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark internationalization via Madrid System
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants can file an international trademark application through the Madrid System, which allows a single application in one language and payment of fees in one currency to seek protection in designated members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite international filing, the decision to issue a registration remains with each designated national/regional office; the Protocol now solely governs the Madrid System. The System also centralizes post-registration management (changes, renewals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial design protection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial designs protect the ornamental or aesthetic aspects of a useful article (lines, colors, three-dimensional forms) and can be protected if they are new or original; rights are territorial and registrations are for a limited term (commonly 15 years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some jurisdictions protect designs via design patents rather than registration; terms and renewal rules vary (e.g., China 10 years from application date). Hague System allows filing up to 100 designs per international application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hague System for industrial designs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hague System makes it possible to register industrial designs in multiple territories by filing a single application with WIPO; it allows up to 100 different designs per application and centralizes subsequent management (changes, renewals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The System comprises the Hague Act and the Geneva Act and simplifies multinational registration though national offices retain substantive control under their laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant variety protection substantive criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A breeder's right is granted only when a plant variety is new, distinct, uniform and stable, and has a suitable denomination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protection is obtained by filing an individual application with each authority entrusted to grant breeders’ rights. In the US, plant varieties may be protected under the Plant Patent Act (asexually reproduced varieties) or the Plant Variety Protection Act (sexually reproduced and tuber-propagated varieties), with statutory exclusions (e.g., fungi, bacteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical indication (GI) function and use-conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: A GI identifies a good as originating in a specific geographical area and possessing a quality, reputation or other characteristic essentially attributable to that origin; it indicates a connection between product quality/characteristics/reputation and territory of origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GIs are mainly used for agricultural and food products but also for handicrafts and manufactured goods whose characteristics derive from traditional skills or local resources. Use of a protected GI is limited to goods that conform to applicable requirements concerning area of origin, processing method and typicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellation of origin stronger geographical link
rubrics_metrics.description: An appellation of origin is a special, more restrictive kind of GI: the quality or characteristics of the product must be due exclusively or essentially to the geographical environment (natural and human factors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellations of origin are a subset of GIs with a stronger required link to territory and often identified by geographical names or traditional denominations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection mechanisms for GIs abroad
rubrics_metrics.description: GIs can be protected abroad through sui generis systems (dedicated GI laws), trademark law (collective and certification marks), unfair competition/consumer protection laws, administrative and judicial decisions, or through regional/bilateral agreements listing protected GIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These systems are not mutually exclusive and often coexist. Protection obtained in one jurisdiction is territorial; international agreements can facilitate protection abroad (e.g., Lisbon System, bilateral lists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lisbon System registration effects and national discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration with the WIPO International Bureau under the Lisbon System ensures protection in all Lisbon contracting parties without the need for renewal and for as long as the appellation or GI remains protected in its country of origin; however each contracting party retains the prerogative to refuse protection on national grounds within one year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Geneva Act (2015) extended the Lisbon System's scope to the general category of GIs and made the System more flexible to accommodate various national protection mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent application and equivalent grant counting (statistical convention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications or grants at regional offices are treated as equivalent to multiple applications/grants—one in each member state—by multiplying each regional application/grant by the number of member states, with specific counting rules for different regional offices (EPO, BOIP, EAPO, OAPI, EUIPO, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For EPO and ARIPO data, special counting applies (counts as one application abroad if applicant not resident, or as one resident and one abroad if applicant resides in a member state). The equivalent concept is used for reporting data by origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application date definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The application date is the date on which an IP office receives an application that meets the minimum requirements (also referred to as the filing date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This date is fundamental for priority, novelty assessment and statistical reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance requirement for IP rights
rubrics_metrics.description: To remain in force, IP protection must be maintained, primarily by paying the required fee to the IP office (maintenance or renewal fees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trademarks can be maintained indefinitely by paying renewal fees; patents, utility models and industrial designs have limited maintenance windows/terms and may lapse if fees are not paid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification systems as assignment criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: International classification systems (IPC for patents, Nice Classification for trademarks, Locarno Classification for industrial designs) assign symbols/classes according to technical features or categories of goods/services and are used to index and compare filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPC symbols can be multiple for a single patent application with multiple technical features. Nice and Locarno classes affect class counts and reporting; offices may use single-class or multi-class filing systems affecting statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microorganism deposit / International Depositary Authority (IDA) role
rubrics_metrics.description: An International Depositary Authority is an institution (typically a culture collection) that receives, accepts, stores and furnishes samples of deposited microorganisms for patent procedure purposes under the Budapest Treaty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As of September 2023, there were 49 IDAs. A deposit made at any IDA recognized under the Treaty suffices for national patent procedures in contracting states.
